explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. "For I will gather all the nations for battle against Jerusalem, and the city will be captured…" (Zechariah 14:2). It's a hard line, friend, and I won't dress it up. But keep reading, because this prophecy has a whole lot more to say.
I get why you'd hope so. But the text says the city "…will be captured…" (Zechariah 14:2). It doesn't say Jerusalem holds them off. The story doesn't stop there, though, so hang on to your apron.

Nice thought, but the prophecy says otherwise. The LORD says He will gather all the nations for battle against Jerusalem, and "…the city will be captured…" (Zechariah 14:2). The verse doesn't say Jerusalem is left alone. It's a heavy part, and I think it's meant to be taken seriously.

Right. The text says "Half of the city will go into exile, but the rest of the people will not be removed from the city." (Zechariah 14:2). So even in the middle of the capture, some people stay put. Half leave, half remain.

Not quite. The text says "Half of the city will go into exile, but the rest of the people will not be removed from the city." (Zechariah 14:2). So the city isn't emptied. Some of its people stay right where they are.

Yes! "Then the LORD will go out to fight against those nations, as He fights in the day of battle." (Zechariah 14:3). No army gets named as the one who steps in. The One who goes out is the LORD Himself. After a verse about a captured city, that's a turn worth noticing, friend.

The text doesn't name any army here. It says "Then the LORD will go out to fight against those nations…" (Zechariah 14:3). The One who goes out is the LORD Himself. Assyria never shows up in this verse.

Good guess if you're picturing history books, but the verse isn't about an army. "Then the LORD will go out to fight against those nations, as He fights in the day of battle." (Zechariah 14:3). The LORD is the one who fights. Persia isn't mentioned.

That's it. "You will flee by My mountain valley, for it will extend to Azal." (Zechariah 14:5). The Mount of Olives is split in two, forming a great valley (Zechariah 14:4). The mountain splits and the valley becomes the way out. That's quite a hallway to have appear out of nowhere.

I like the thinking, but treasure isn't in this verse. The text says "You will flee by My mountain valley…" (Zechariah 14:5). The valley is a way to run through, not a hiding spot. Nobody's stashing anything.
Folks aren't setting up house here. The text says "You will flee by My mountain valley, for it will extend to Azal." (Zechariah 14:5). They're fleeing through it. Nobody's hanging a welcome mat.

Yes! "Then the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with Him." (Zechariah 14:5). He arrives with company. The text doesn't tell us more than that, so I won't either. It comes right after the verse about fleeing through the valley.

Kings, huh? Crowns, capes, the whole parade, I like where your head's at, friend. But this verse lists no kings. It says "Then the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with Him." (Zechariah 14:5). The ones with Him are called the holy ones, and the text stops there. Even my mustache can't add names the verse doesn't give.

No elders are named here. The text says "Then the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with Him." (Zechariah 14:5). Those who come with Him are the holy ones. I'd read that line twice just to enjoy it.

Close, but this day breaks the pattern. The text says "It will be a unique day known only to the LORD, without day or night; but when evening comes, there will be light." (Zechariah 14:7). So evening comes, and light comes with it. My own kitchen goes dark at evening, so this one gets me.

Correct. "but when evening comes, there will be light." (Zechariah 14:7). It's a unique day known only to the LORD, without day or night. Evening shows up and the light shows up with it. That's not the usual order at all.

Yes. "…living water will flow out from Jerusalem, half of it toward the Eastern Sea and the other half toward the Western Sea, in summer and winter alike." (Zechariah 14:8). Half of it heads toward each sea. Any season, it keeps flowing. I've never had an oven that steady.
This one is true. The text says the living water will flow "…in summer and winter alike." (Zechariah 14:8). It flows out from Jerusalem toward both seas, and the seasons don't stop it.

That's the word. "On that day the LORD will become King over all the earth…" (Zechariah 14:9). Not over one city or one land, but all the earth. The verse goes on, "…the LORD alone, and His name alone." (Zechariah 14:9).

Nice word, but it's not the one in this verse. The text says the LORD "…will become King over all the earth…" (Zechariah 14:9). King is what the prophecy calls Him here. And it says over all the earth.

Priest is a fine job, friend, but this verse reaches for a much bigger one. "On that day the LORD will become King over all the earth…" (Zechariah 14:9). All the earth! I can barely keep one bakery counter in order, and that's my whole territory. Then the verse adds "…the LORD alone, and His name alone." (Zechariah 14:9).
The text says the opposite. "…the LORD alone, and His name alone." (Zechariah 14:9). That means no sharing. No gods of the nations are on the throne with Him.
Right. The verse says "…the LORD alone, and His name alone." (Zechariah 14:9). He becomes King over all the earth, and the nations' gods are not mentioned as sharing it. The word is alone.

Good news, friend, it's the other way around. The text says "People will live there, and never again will there be an utter destruction." (Zechariah 14:11). So no second round of utter destruction is coming for the raised up city.

Yes, False is right, baker. The text says "People will live there, and never again will there be an utter destruction. So Jerusalem will dwell securely." (Zechariah 14:11). Just before that, the city "…will be raised up and will remain in her place…" (Zechariah 14:10). Never again is a big promise, and the city dwells securely. So no second round of utter destruction is coming.

explanations.answer: They will turn on each other
explanations.explanation: That's right. The text says "…each will seize the hand of another, and the hand of one will rise against the other." (Zechariah 14:13). The panic comes from the LORD. This is another heavy part, and it's okay to let it sit.

explanations.answer: They will grow calm and wait
explanations.explanation: The text describes the opposite. It says "…a great panic from the LORD will come upon them…" (Zechariah 14:13). Calm isn't in the verse. Instead, "…each will seize the hand of another, and the hand of one will rise against the other."

explanations.answer: They will make peace with Judah
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't go that way. The panic comes from the LORD, and "…the hand of one will rise against the other." (Zechariah 14:13). They turn on one another. Judah fights at Jerusalem in the next verse (Zechariah 14:14).

explanations.answer: It will be collected in great abundance
explanations.explanation: Yes. "…the wealth of all the surrounding nations will be collected—gold, silver, and apparel in great abundance." (Zechariah 14:14). That's gold, silver and clothing, piled up. It's in the same verse that says Judah will also fight at Jerusalem. I've never seen a cookie box that full.

explanations.answer: It will be scattered across the land
explanations.explanation: Scattered, like crumbs off a cookie tray? I see the picture, friend, but the verse says the opposite. The wealth "…will be collected…" (Zechariah 14:14). Gathered up, not scattered, and the text names gold, silver and apparel in great abundance.

explanations.answer: It will all be sent back home
explanations.explanation: Not in this prophecy. The text says the wealth of all the surrounding nations "…will be collected…" (Zechariah 14:14). It names gold, silver and apparel in great abundance. Nothing here says it's sent back.

That's the turn. "Then all the survivors from the nations that came against Jerusalem will go up year after year to worship the King, the LORD of Hosts…" (Zechariah 14:16). Survivors from the very nations that came against Jerusalem are the ones going up to worship. And they go year after year.
Walls aren't mentioned in this verse. The text says the survivors "…will go up year after year to worship the King, the LORD of Hosts…" (Zechariah 14:16). Their trip is about worship.

You'd expect that, wouldn't you? But the verse says the survivors from the nations that came against Jerusalem "…will go up year after year to worship the King, the LORD of Hosts…" (Zechariah 14:16). They go up to worship.

Yes. They go up "…to worship the King, the LORD of Hosts, and to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles." (Zechariah 14:16). The prophecy names it again in verses 18 and 19. So this feast is no side note here.
That's a real feast in Scripture (Exodus 34:22), but it isn't the one here. The text says they go up "…to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles." (Zechariah 14:16). That's the feast this prophecy names.

That's a real feast too (Exodus 23:15), but it isn't the one in this verse. Zechariah says they go up "…to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles." (Zechariah 14:16). That's the feast named, and it's named again later in the passage.

That's it. The text says "And should any of the families of the earth not go up to Jerusalem to worship the King, the LORD of Hosts, then the rain will not fall on them." (Zechariah 14:17). The rain is what's held back. It's about families of the earth, not just one nation.

Manna is real in Scripture. The LORD promised bread from heaven for Israel (Exodus 16:4), and Israel called that bread manna (Exodus 16:31). But this verse isn't about manna. It says "…then the rain will not fall on them." (Zechariah 14:17).
Fire isn't in this verse. The text says "…then the rain will not fall on them." (Zechariah 14:17). The rain is what doesn't fall.

explanations.answer: The sprinkling bowls before the altar
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's it. "…the cooking pots in the house of the LORD will be like the sprinkling bowls before the altar." (Zechariah 14:20). The everyday pots are put right alongside those bowls, and that's a big step up for a cooking pot. Then verse 21 says every pot in Jerusalem and Judah will be holy to the LORD of Hosts.

explanations.answer: The water jars beside the well
explanations.explanation: Water jars by the well sound lovely, friend, and I'd have picked them too, mostly because I'm thirsty. But the text says the cooking pots "…will be like the sprinkling bowls before the altar." (Zechariah 14:20). The comparison is to the bowls by the altar, not to anything out by the well. So those plain cooking pots get a big step up from the kitchen.

explanations.answer: The clay jars in the storeroom
explanations.explanation: A storeroom is a sensible guess, friend, but this verse doesn't send those pots to the back. It says "…the cooking pots in the house of the LORD will be like the sprinkling bowls before the altar." (Zechariah 14:20). Picture my plain old mixing bowl getting a front-row seat beside the fancy serving tray, and everybody treating it with respect. I'd be crying into the dough. That's the jump here: ordinary pots, set right alongside the bowls before the altar.

Yes. The last line of the passage says "And on that day there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of the LORD of Hosts." (Zechariah 14:21). That's how the passage ends. The text doesn't say more than that.
Look at the last line again. "And on that day there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of the LORD of Hosts." (Zechariah 14:21). So this one is true. That's the way the prophecy closes.
